\small\color{hrmadark}
\textbf{Scope.} HRMA is software for the preliminary design and analysis of
rocket motors, built on closed-form and one-dimensional engineering relations.
It is not a flight-qualification tool. Results must be confirmed by physical
testing before flight (Section~\ref{sec:kapsam}).

\medskip
\textbf{Basis of results.} Every value on screen comes from user input, from
data with a stated source or from the model's solution. If a required input is
missing, the calculation stops and names the missing field. When a default
value is used, it is reported with its name and source. Outside the model's
validity limits no verdict is issued and the reason is shown.
\end{notkutu}
\end{titlepage}

\section{General Information}\label{sec:genel}

\subsection{Purpose and scope}

HRMA is a desktop application for the preliminary design and analysis of
hybrid, solid and liquid rocket motors. From the requirement and design
parameters supplied by the user it computes the motor geometry, its
performance and a list of warnings; it runs thermal, structural, flow,
stability, feed-system, safety and uncertainty analyses on the same motor;
and it exports the result as a report (PDF, XLSX), CAD (STEP, STL, DXF),
engineering drawings and a flight-simulation file (\kod{.eng}).

The intended users are engineers and teams who design motors: rocketry teams,
research groups, companies developing motors. The guide assumes familiarity
with the basic concepts of rocket propulsion (thrust, specific impulse,
oxidizer-to-fuel ratio, nozzle expansion); definitions are in
Appendix~\ref{sec:ekb}, symbols in Appendix~\ref{sec:ekc}.

\subsection{Basis of results and validity checks}\label{sec:ilke}

When HRMA cannot compute a quantity it shows no value for it. This behaviour is
called fail-closed and appears on screen in four forms.

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering\small
\caption{Forms of fail-closed behaviour on screen}\label{tab:kapali}
\begin{tabular}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{3.6cm}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{6.4cm}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{5.6cm}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Form} & \textbf{On screen} & \textbf{Example (from this guide's examples)} \\
\midrule
Rejection by name & The request is not sent, or the server rejects it with 422; the missing or out-of-range field is named by its on-screen label. & In the Nozzle Flow panel an empty \ui{Chamber Pressure} is rejected with ``incomplete\_flow\_input'' naming the field. \\
Declared default & The value used for a field left empty is listed with its name and reason. & In the hybrid example, the list \ui{VALUES THIS RUN ASSUMED FOR FIELDS YOU LEFT EMPTY}: \ui{Combustion (c*) Efficiency = 89\%}. \\
Withheld verdict & No verdict is issued; ``NOT EVALUATED'' (``NOT\_EVALUATED'' in the dock panels), ``VERDICT WITHHELD'' or ``NOT MODELLED'' is shown with the reason. & In the hybrid example the wall was sized by HRMA, so the structural verdict is \ui{NOT EVALUATED} and \ui{VERDICT WITHHELD}. \\
Provenance line & The source of a published number is written next to it: user input, solver result or sourced default. & \ui{c* efficiency $\eta_{c^*}$ = 0.89 (sourced default: median of 26 measured firings, range 0.77-0.99)}. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Warnings are not a sign of malfunction; they report a model limit or a design
approaching a limit. Numbers are read together with their warnings
(Section~\ref{sec:hukumler}).

\subsection{Structure and conventions of this guide}

The guide has two parts.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em]
  \item \textbf{Part I, Getting started and worked examples.} Installation, a
  15-minute quick start, and a step-by-step study of the example shipped for
  each motor type. Each step states what to look at on screen and the
  physical meaning of the number.
  \item \textbf{Part II, Reference.} Purpose, inputs, outputs, verdicts,
  warnings and limits of every page, in tables. The input tables are generated
  from the application's own screen: label, identifier, unit, form limit,
  default and the ``?'' note next to the field.
\end{itemize}

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering\small
\caption{Conventions}\label{tab:yazim}
\begin{tabular}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{4.2cm}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{11.4cm}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Item} & \textbf{Convention} \\
\midrule
Interface names & Labels, buttons and tabs are written \ui{in this typeface} exactly as on screen. \\
Field identifier & The name used in the project file (\kod{.hrma}) and in server messages is written \kod{in this typeface} (example: \kod{chamber\_\allowbreak{}pressure}). Identifier to page: Appendix~\ref{sec:ekd}. \\
Units & SI. Pressures are absolute and in bar unless stated otherwise. \\
Numbers & The English text uses a decimal point (209.8~s). Example numbers were read from the screen of the version this guide describes (3.0.5). \\
Procedures & Numbered steps; each step gives the action and the expected result. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\subsection{Local operation and data privacy}

Design data never leaves the computer. The Python runtime and all libraries are
inside the installer. On its own the application goes online only for the
new-version check at startup (GitHub); if the request fails the application
works normally, and the check can be switched off in \ui{Settings}. The
following accesses are started by the user:

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.6em]
  \item \ui{Update now}: the installer is downloaded to the Downloads folder
  (Section~\ref{sec:guncelleme}).
  \item \ui{Report a bug} and the GitHub links of the window menu: the GitHub
  page opens; submitting the issue is the user's decision.
  \item The online enrichment on the Launch Site page: satellite tiles (NASA
  GIBS) and elevation and surface weather data (Open-Meteo). Both are off by
  default; when enabled, the request sends the coordinates of the viewed region
  to the provider.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Installation and Start-up}\label{sec:kurulum}

\subsection{System requirements}

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering\small
\caption{Supported platforms and installers}\label{tab:platform}
\begin{tabular}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{3.2cm}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{5.0cm}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{7.4cm}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Platform} & \textbf{Package} & \textbf{Note} \\
\midrule
Windows 10/11 (64-bit) & \kod{HRMA-Setup-3.0.5.exe} & Per-user installation, no administrator rights needed. The package is unsigned; a SmartScreen warning may appear. \\
macOS 11 or later, Apple Silicon & \kod{HRMA-Setup-3.0.5-macOS.dmg} & Does not run on Intel Macs. The package is unsigned; Gatekeeper asks for approval at first launch. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The Python 3.12 runtime and all dependencies (thermochemistry, CAD kernel,
plotting libraries) are inside the package; nothing else needs to be installed.

\subsection{Installation procedure}

\textbf{Windows}
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.6em]
  \item Run \kod{HRMA-Setup-3.0.5.exe}. Press \ui{Next} on the welcome page,
  \ui{Install} on the folder page and \ui{Finish} on the last page. If
  \ui{Launch HRMA now} is ticked on the last page, the application opens.
  \item The installation folder must be empty or contain a previous HRMA
  installation; if an unrelated folder is chosen, setup does not proceed and
  asks for another folder. The default folder is
  \kod{\%LOCALAPPDATA\%\textbackslash{}HRMA}.
  \item If SmartScreen warns, press \ui{More info}, then \ui{Run anyway}.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{macOS}
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.6em]
  \item Open \kod{HRMA-Setup-3.0.5-macOS.dmg}.
  \item Drag the \kod{HRMA} icon to the \kod{Applications} folder.
  \item At first launch right-click the application (or Control-click it),
  choose \ui{Open} and press \ui{Open} again in the dialog. If the dialog has
  no \ui{Open} button, press \ui{Open Anyway} at the bottom of \ui{System
  Settings} → \ui{Privacy \& Security}. This approval is requested only once.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{First launch and project directory}

The application shows a splash screen while the calculation engines load,
then opens the home page in its own window. If the application is launched
again while it is running, no second calculation server is started: the
launcher finds the running application and connects the new window to it. Both
windows use the same projects and the same calculation engine. When the first
window is closed, the application closes.

Projects are stored as \kod{.hrma} files in the user's
\kod{Documents/\allowbreak{}HRMA/\allowbreak{}projects} directory. At first launch three example
projects are copied there (Table~\ref{tab:ornekler}). They are copied once; a
deleted example does not come back, and a copy the user has modified is never
overwritten. An unmodified copy of an older example is refreshed with the
current example in a new version.

\centering\small
\caption{Example projects shipped with the application (3.0.5)}\label{tab:ornekler}
\begin{tabular}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{4.6cm}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{6.6cm}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{4.4cm}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Project name} & \textbf{Design} & \textbf{Main result on screen} \\
\midrule
\kod{Example Hybrid N2O-HTPB 3kN} & N\textsubscript{2}O/HTPB hybrid, 3000~N, 10~s, 30~bar, O/F 6.0, showerhead injector & Isp 209.8~s (design point); $I_t$ 29\,956~N·s \\
\kod{Example Solid KNDX BATES 75mm} & KNDX solid, 3 BATES grains 75/32/360~mm (cartridge-loaded), 40~bar design pressure, graphite nozzle & Isp 125.3~s (sea level); peak thrust 1498~N; $I_t$ 2957~N·s \\
\kod{Example Liquid LOX-RP1 25kN} & LOX/RP-1 liquid, 25~kN, 50~bar, O/F 2.0, gas-generator cycle, regenerative cooling, 1.0~mm CuCrZr liner and closeout shell, 30~s burn (example input) & Isp 257.1~s (sea level), 301.1~s (vacuum); $I_t$ 750\,000~N·s \\

Output files (reports, CAD, drawings, \kod{.eng}, packages) are delivered as
downloads. In the application window every download opens a save dialog; the
dialog starts in the Downloads folder with the suggested file name, and the
location and name are chosen there. The \ui{Open Output Folder} item of the
application menu opens the \kod{Documents/\allowbreak{}HRMA} folder; it holds
the project files (\kod{projects}). Downloaded files are not written to this
folder automatically. The application log is \kod{hrma\_\allowbreak{}log.txt}
in the same folder on Windows and
\kod{\textasciitilde/\allowbreak{}Library/\allowbreak{}Logs/\allowbreak{}HRMA.log} on macOS; attach it when
reporting a problem.

\subsection{Updates}\label{sec:guncelleme}

When a new version is found at startup, a window offers three options.

\begin{table}[htbp]

\section{Getting Started: the First 15 Minutes}\label{sec:ilk15}

This section uses the hybrid example shipped with the application to open a
motor, calculate it, read the results, change one input, and obtain the report
and the CAD file. Section~\ref{sec:uyg-hibrit} explains each screen in detail.

\subsection{Procedure}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.6em]
  \item \textbf{Open the hybrid designer.} On the home page press
  \ui{LAUNCH DESIGNER} on the \ui{Hybrid Motors} card. The hybrid page opens
  with an empty form (Figure~\ref{fig:hib-acilis}).

  \item \textbf{Load the example.} In the project bar press \ui{Open} and select
  \kod{Example Hybrid N2O-HTPB 3kN}. The form fills with the example's inputs.
  The same example also opens from the \ui{RECENT PROJECTS} list on the home
  page.

  \item \textbf{Calculate.} Press \ui{Calculate} below the form. The result
  sections open below the form. Calculation time depends on the computer; in
  the measurement for this guide the hybrid example finished in 15~s.

  \item \textbf{Read the headline numbers.} The \ui{PERFORMANCE SUMMARY}
  cards: \ui{ISP (DESIGN POINT, AT DESIGN-ALTITUDE AMBIENT)} 209.8~s,
  \ui{THRUST} 3000~N, \ui{CHAMBER PRESSURE} 30.0~bar, \ui{MASS FLOW RATE}
  1.458~kg/s. Thrust and chamber pressure are inputs; Isp and mass flow are
  solved. Check: $\dot m = F/(I_{sp}\,g_0) = 3000/(209.8 \times 9.80665) =
  1.458$~kg/s.

  \item \textbf{Read the strip at the top of the results.} The strip says
  \ui{6 physics items are NOT modelled in this hybrid result}; expanding it
  lists what the model does not compute for this motor. The fifth card of the
  \ui{PERFORMANCE SUMMARY}, \ui{STRUCTURAL MIN SF}, reads \ui{NOT
  EVALUATED} and \ui{WALL: SIZED BY HRMA}; the verdict line under the wall
  block is \ui{VERDICT WITHHELD}. No wall thickness was entered, so HRMA sized
  the wall and does not accept the wall it sized itself
  (Section~\ref{sec:hib-cidar}).

  \item \textbf{Read the warnings.} The \ui{WARNINGS} section of this example
  carries nine \ui{WARNING} lines and four \ui{INFO} lines, and no
  \ui{CRITICAL} line. Each line names a quantity, its limit and the change that
  can be made.

  \item \textbf{Change one input.} In the \ui{MIXTURE RATIO} section raise
  \ui{O/F Ratio} from 6 to 7 and press \ui{Calculate} again. Isp rises from
  209.8 to 210.1~s; a \ui{CRITICAL} line is added to \ui{WARNINGS}:
  \ui{The throat wall reaches 3304 K, above the 3300 K allowable temperature of
  Graphite (isostatic, nozzle insert grade) \ldots{}}. As the mixture ratio approaches stoichiometric the flame
  temperature rises; the Isp curve is flat in this region but the thermal load
  on the nozzle throat increases. Set the value back to 6 and calculate again.

  \item \textbf{Get the report.} In \ui{EXPORT \& CAD OPTIONS} at the bottom of
  the page press \ui{Summary PDF} or \ui{Technical PDF} in the \ui{Analysis
  Reports} group. \ui{Export Results} at the top of the results produces the
  same file as \ui{Summary PDF}.

  \item \textbf{Get the CAD file.} In the \ui{3D CAD Design} group of the same
  section press \ui{Generate 3D Model}; in the \ui{Download Package} window
  choose \ui{Download CAD Files (STEP)}. To get STEP, DXF, the drawing PDF and
  STL files in one archive use \ui{Generate All Files} in the \ui{Complete
  Package} group (Section~\ref{sec:disaaktarim}).

  \item \textbf{Save the project.} To keep the modified design under your own
  name press \ui{Save As} in the project bar.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Purpose}

\ekran{img/v3_0_5/hibrit_form_temel_en.png}{\ui{BASIC PARAMETERS} after loading the example hybrid: thrust, burn time, chamber pressure and tank pressure source.}{fig:u1-form}

\subsection{Performance: why Isp is 209.8~s}

After calculation the \ui{PERFORMANCE SUMMARY} shows four headline cards and the \ui{STRUCTURAL MIN SF} card
(Figure~\ref{fig:hib-ozet}). Isp is the product of the thrust coefficient and
the delivered characteristic velocity:

\[
I_{sp} = \frac{c^*\,C_F}{g_0} = \frac{1423 \times 1.445}{9.80665} = 209.7~\text{s}
\]

The 209.8~s on screen comes from the unrounded values; the product of the
rounded $c^*$ and $C_F$ shown on screen gives 209.7~s.

The provenance line below the cards gives the source of $c^*$: \ui{delivered c*
1423 m/s = $\eta_{c^*}$ × theoretical 1599 m/s}. The theoretical value comes
from equilibrium thermochemistry (Cantera) at the chamber pressure and O/F 6.0.
In a real hybrid chamber mixing is incomplete and combustion does not finish;
the $c^*$ efficiency carries this loss. $\eta_{c^*} = 0.89$ is the median of 26
measured N\textsubscript{2}O/HTPB firings in HRMA's validation records (range
0.77--0.99). The field was left empty, so this value was used and declared in
the \ui{VALUES THIS RUN ASSUMED FOR FIELDS YOU LEFT EMPTY} list. If you have
your own measurement, enter it in \ui{Combustion (c*) Efficiency (\%)}; Isp,
mass flow and propellant masses are recomputed with it.

The thrust coefficient $C_F = 1.445$ follows from the expansion ratio
$\varepsilon = 5.0$ and the ambient pressure at the design altitude. Because
\ui{Ae/At Ratio} was entered as 0 the model solved the ratio that makes the
exit pressure equal to ambient (5.0364); the warning list says so with
\ui{Input field 'Ae/At Ratio' (0) is solved by the model, not read from the
form}.

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering\small
\caption{Hybrid example numbers in \ui{MOTOR DESIGN} and \ui{DESIGN REPORT}}\label{tab:u1-cikti}

\subsection{Design point and tank blowdown}

The headline numbers belong to the \emph{regulated} design point: the oxidizer
flow is taken as constant through the burn. The example, however, uses a
self-pressurised N\textsubscript{2}O tank whose pressure falls as it empties.
The result section reports this on a separate line: \ui{impulse 26789 N·s (89 \%
of the headline), burn time 10.45 s, end: OXIDIZER DEPLETED}. The link on the
line leads to the \ui{Tank Blowdown} panel, which plots tank pressure, flow and
thrust against time. For the true total impulse of a self-pressurised design
the panel's number is used.

\ekran{img/v3_0_5/hibrit_tank_bosalmasi_en.png}{The \ui{Tank Blowdown} panel: pressure, flow and thrust decay of the self-pressurised N\textsubscript{2}O tank. Note the end reason and the total impulse.}{fig:u1-tank}

\subsection{Chamber wall: three zones}\label{sec:hib-cidar}

The \ui{CHAMBER WALL: THREE ZONES (HYBRID)} block evaluates the wall in three zones.

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering\small
\caption{Wall zones in the hybrid example}\label{tab:u1-cidar}
\begin{tabular}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{4.0cm}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{3.6cm}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{8.0cm}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Zone} & \textbf{Verdict} & \textbf{Reason} \\
\midrule
Under the fuel grain (1125.0~mm) & \ui{PROTECTED DURING BURN} & The fuel covers the case; case temperature 293.15~K (declared, not computed). With residual web 0 the case is uncovered at the end of the burn; this tail-off exposure was not evaluated. \\
Pre-combustion chamber (42.1~mm) & \ui{LINER REQUIRED} & Without a liner the bare wall reaches 3257~K in steady state; HRMA sized a 2.12~mm insulation liner. \\
Post-combustion chamber (25.2~mm) & \ui{LINER REQUIRED} & Same reason and same liner thickness. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The same block gives the structural verdict as \ui{STRUCTURE: NOT EVALUATED}
and \ui{VERDICT WITHHELD}. Reason: no wall thickness was entered, so HRMA sized
the wall itself to meet the target safety factor. The reported safety factor is
then the target read back, not an independent verification; the screen states
\ui{This result is a DESIGN PROPOSAL}. To obtain a structural verdict, enter the
real thickness of the wall to be manufactured; HRMA then tests that wall.

\subsection{Reading the warnings}

The warning list carries lines of four classes (Table~\ref{tab:siddet}). The
example has no \ui{CRITICAL} line; it has nine \ui{WARNING} and four
\ui{INFO} lines. The engineer asks the same question on each line: under which
assumption did the number come out, and does that assumption hold for this
design.

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering\small
\caption{Warnings of the hybrid example and how to read them}\label{tab:u1-uyari}
\begin{tabular}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{6.4cm}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{9.2cm}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Warning (summary)} & \textbf{Meaning and possible action} \\
\midrule
Injector Reynolds number 1\,197\,894 exceeds 200\,000, the upper bound of the correlation range. & The discharge-coefficient correlation is extrapolated for this flow; a measured $C_d$ can be entered in \ui{Injector Discharge Coefficient (-)}. \\
Injector pressure drop is 0.68 of chamber pressure. & In a self-pressurised N\textsubscript{2}O tank the drop is not chosen; it is the vapour pressure minus chamber pressure. To lower it, lower the tank temperature or raise the chamber pressure. \\
Built-in HTPB regression coefficients are biased against the validation database (median bias $-$39.5\,\% over 43 own records). & The known bias of the regression prediction; the coefficients were deliberately not retuned. Enter $a$ and $n$ from your own firing data. \\
Grain L/D 13.4 and chamber L/D 14.2 exceed the single-port practice threshold of 10. & The motor has become a long, thin tube. Increase the port count or enlarge the port diameter (the design $G_{ox}$ falls). \\
Pre- and post-combustion chamber bare wall 3257~K; 2.12~mm liner needed. & Table~\ref{tab:u1-cidar}. \\
\ui{'Ae/At Ratio'} and \ui{'Chamber Diameter (mm)'} fields (0) are not read from the form. & 0 means ``let the model solve it''; the analysis uses its solved values 5.0364 and 84.1362. \\
Injector L/D 1.2 outside the 3--5 band (HRMA heuristic threshold). & Plate thickness and hole diameter together set L/D; the hydraulic-flip verdict is sensitive to L/D. \\
Target injection velocity 30.0~m/s is not set by hole count; achieved 42.7~m/s. & The velocity follows from flow and the pressure drop solved by the circuit; the $\Delta P$ needed for the target (5.81~bar) is stated on the line. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

example. Note the class of each line (\ui{WARNING}, \ui{INFO}) and the change
proposed at the end of the line.}{fig:hib-uyari}

\ekran{img/v3_0_5/hibrit_kesit_en.png}{Motor cross-section: chamber, fuel grain, injector plate and nozzle dimensions. Note the ratio of grain length to chamber diameter (L/D).}{fig:u1-kesit}

\subsection{A long fuel grain: the single-port L/D warning}\label{sec:u1-ld}

The line in the example's warning list: \ui{Grain L/D = 13.4 and chamber L/D =
14.2 exceed the single-port design-practice threshold of 10: the motor is an
unusually long, thin tube.} In a single-port hybrid the fuel flow
comes from the port surface: $\dot m_f = \rho_f\,\pi\,D_p\,L\,r$. The
regression rate is small (0.84~mm/s on average in the example), so the
required fuel flow is reached only with a long port; in the example the grain
is 1125.0~mm long and 84.1~mm in diameter. This is the reason for moving to a
multi-port grain (Sutton and Biblarz, Ch.~16). The threshold of 10 is an
engineering-practice threshold used by HRMA; it is not a single published
constant, and the warning states it as a number.

The effect of the two changes the line proposes was measured on the example by
changing one field at a time (Table~\ref{tab:u1-ld}). \ui{Number of Ports} and
\ui{Initial Port Diameter (mm)} are in the \ui{ADVANCED PARAMETERS} section.

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering\small
\caption{Two changes against the single-port L/D warning (hybrid example, from the screen)}\label{tab:u1-ld}
\begin{tabular}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{4.0cm}rrrrrrl@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Change} & \textbf{Grain} & \textbf{Outer} & \textbf{L/D} & \textbf{Total} & \textbf{Dry} & \textbf{Isp} & \textbf{Warn-} \\
 & \textbf{length} & \textbf{dia.} & & \textbf{length} & \textbf{mass} & & \textbf{ing} \\
 & mm & mm & -- & mm & kg & s & \\
\midrule
Example (1 port, automatic) & 1125.0 & 84.1 & 13.37 & 1309.6 & 13.28 & 209.8 & yes \\
\ui{Number of Ports} 2 & 795.8 & 127.4 & 6.25 & 1052.5 & 23.43 & 209.6 & no \\
\ui{Number of Ports} 3 & 650.1 & 117.4 & 5.54 & 890.2 & 16.94 & 209.4 & no \\
\ui{Number of Ports} 4 & 563.1 & 118.1 & 4.77 & 804.4 & 15.45 & 209.3 & no \\
\ui{Initial Port Diameter} 80~mm & 1146.2 & 94.3 & 12.15 & 1347.7 & 16.96 & 209.8 & yes \\
\ui{Initial Port Diameter} 95~mm & 1167.9 & 107.1 & 10.90 & 1390.8 & 22.33 & 209.9 & yes \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Increasing the port count shortens the grain: the same fuel flow comes from
more burning surface. Two ports bring L/D down to 6.25, but the outer diameter
grows to 127.4~mm and the dry mass to 23.43~kg; three and four ports give a
shorter and lighter motor. Enlarging the port alone is not enough: the initial
oxidizer mass flux drops, the regression rate falls and the grain gets longer
(1146.2~mm at 80~mm). L/D falls only because the outer diameter grows, and at
95~mm it is still above the threshold. With a multi-port grain the result
carries an \ui{INFO} line: the ports are modelled as equivalent circular
channels; interaction between channels, web thickness and channel merging are
not modelled. These items are verified by test. Isp stays within 0.5~s in every
case; the decision rests on length, diameter and mass.

\subsection{Changing one input: O/F 6.0 → 7.0}\label{sec:u1-of}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.6em]
  \item In the \ui{MIXTURE RATIO} section type 7 in \ui{O/F Ratio}.
  \item Press \ui{Calculate}.
  \item Compare the results (Table~\ref{tab:u1-of}).
\end{enumerate}

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering\small
\caption{Effect of the O/F change (hybrid example, from the screen)}\label{tab:u1-of}
\begin{tabular}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{5.6cm}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{3.2cm}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{3.2cm}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Quantity} & \textbf{O/F 6.0} & \textbf{O/F 7.0} \\
\midrule
Isp (design point) & 209.8~s & 210.1~s \\
Mass flow & 1.458~kg/s & 1.456~kg/s \\
Delivered / theoretical $c^*$ & 1423 / 1599~m/s & 1421 / 1597~m/s \\
\ui{CRITICAL} lines & none & 1 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Isp barely changes: the N\textsubscript{2}O/HTPB Isp curve is flat in this
region. The flame temperature, however, rises and so does the thermal load on
the nozzle throat. The new \ui{CRITICAL} line: \ui{The throat wall reaches 3304
K, above the 3300 K allowable temperature of Graphite (isostatic, nozzle insert
grade) with Natural (heat sink) cooling. This throat will fail}. The line
offers two remedies: a nozzle material with a higher allowable temperature, or
cooling. A small performance gain has produced a design that exceeds a
material limit; this is why the example runs at O/F 6.0. Set the value back to
6 and calculate again.

\ekran{img/v3_0_5/hibrit_of7_kritik_en.png}{\ui{WARNINGS} of the hybrid example calculated with O/F 7.0: the \ui{CRITICAL} line at the end of the list (throat wall 3304~K, allowable 3300~K). Note in the same list that the fuel grain L/D drops from 13.4 to 11.5: a higher O/F means a lower fuel flow at the same thrust, hence a shorter grain.}{fig:u1-of7}

\subsection{Analysis Dock: the Nozzle Flow panel}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.6em]
  \item In the \ui{ANALYSIS DOCK} below the results open the \ui{FLOW} tab.
  \item The fields of the \ui{Nozzle Flow} panel are filled from the last
  calculation; the badge next to each field reads \ui{COMPUTED} or
  \ui{ASSUMED} (Table~\ref{tab:rozet}).
  \item Press \ui{Run Analysis}.
  \item Read the regime label first: \ui{PERFECT EXPANSION}. The exit pressure
  equals ambient; this is expected, because $\varepsilon$ was solved against
  the ambient pressure.
  \item Compare \ui{CF EFFECTIVE} with the main result: the panel gives
  1.445, the same as the thrust coefficient of the main result. If the two
  differed, the two calculations would be solving different operating points.
  \item Do not mistake the \ui{IDEAL} cards for the motor's numbers. These
  cards are the quasi-1D solution of the chamber state with a $c^*$ efficiency
  and a throat discharge coefficient of 1 (\ui{IDEAL THRUST} 3150~N,
  \ui{IDEAL MASS FLOW} 1.323~kg/s, \ui{IDEAL C*} 1602~m/s). The numbers the
  motor delivers are printed unchanged in the \ui{Delivered by the motor - the
  numbers of the main result} block below: \ui{THRUST (MOTOR)} 3000~N,
  \ui{MASS FLOW (MOTOR)} 1.458~kg/s, \ui{C* DELIVERED (MOTOR)} 1423~m/s,
  \ui{C\_F (MOTOR)} 1.445. The difference is the $c^*$ efficiency (0.89;
  Section~\ref{sec:uyg-hibrit}).
\end{enumerate}

\ekran{img/v3_0_5/hibrit_guverte_akis_en.png}{\ui{Nozzle Flow} panel of the hybrid example after the run: regime label, the \ui{IDEAL} cards and, below them, the numbers the motor delivers. Note that \ui{CF EFFECTIVE} and \ui{C\_F (MOTOR)} are the same.}{fig:u1-akis}

The panel inputs are in Table~\ref{tab:p-akis}; the panel verdicts are in
Section~\ref{sec:guverte}.

\subsection{Report and CAD}

The report and the CAD files are obtained with steps 8 and 9 of
Section~\ref{sec:ilk15}. Exports use the geometry published by the main
calculation; if the geometry is incomplete or a gate is closed, no file is
produced and the reason is given (Section~\ref{sec:disaaktarim}).

\section{Example 2: Solid Motor (KNDX, 3 × BATES 75~mm)}\label{sec:uyg-kati}

\subsection{Purpose}

Read the link between burning area and pressure (Kn), the shape of the thrust
curve, and the two-phase and throat-erosion declarations on the solid example;
change the design pressure and see how burn time and thrust change. The full
input list is in Tables~\ref{tab:kati-0}--\ref{tab:kati-yorunge}.

\subsection{The example}

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering\small
\caption{Main inputs of the solid example (\kod{Example Solid KNDX BATES 75mm})}\label{tab:u2-girdi}
\begin{tabular}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{5.0cm}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{4.0cm}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{6.6cm}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Input} & \textbf{Value} & \textbf{Note} \\
\midrule
\ui{Propellant (catalogue record)} & KNDX (KNO\textsubscript{3}/dextrose 65/35) & Thermochemistry source: catalogue; $\rho$ 1850~kg/m\textsuperscript{3}. \\
\ui{Grain Type}, count & BATES, 3 & Outer surface inhibited; end faces open. \\
\ui{Grain Support} & \ui{Cartridge-loaded (free-standing)} & The grain is cast outside the case and inserted; cure shrinkage is not restrained. Changes only the grain structural results (bore strain, strain safety factor), not the ballistics. \\
Outer diameter / core / length & 75 / 32 / 360~mm & The length is the total length of the grain stack: 3 × 120~mm (the cross-section also shows 2 × 2~mm gaps). \\
\ui{Chamber Pressure (bar)} & 40~bar & Design pressure; the throat is sized for it. \\
\ui{Burn Rate Preset} & \ui{KNDX --- KNO3/Dextrose 65/35 (Nakka fit)} & Piecewise law: 5 pressure regimes. \\
\ui{Nozzle Material} & \ui{Graphite (isostatic, nozzle insert grade)} & Convergent 45°, divergent 15°. \\
\ui{Case Material} & \ui{Carbon steel (generic, A36-class)} & \ui{Yield Strength $\sigma_y$ (MPa)}: the screen states that the material value 250 was applied because the field was not supplied. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\subsection{Performance and Kn}

The \ui{PERFORMANCE SUMMARY} shows ten cards: \ui{SEA LEVEL ISP} 125.3~s,
\ui{VACUUM ISP} 141.5~s, \ui{AVERAGE THRUST} 1299~N, \ui{PEAK THRUST} 1498~N,
\ui{PEAK CHAMBER PRESSURE} 40.0~bar, \ui{BURN TIME} 2.28~s, \ui{TOTAL IMPULSE}
3.0~kN·s, \ui{C* EFFICIENCY} 95.0\,\%, \ui{THRUST COEFFICIENT} 1.41,
\ui{PROPELLANT MASS} 2.41~kg.

The Isp of KNDX is low because its flame temperature is low and its products
have a high molar mass; $c^*$ scales approximately with
$\sqrt{T_c/\mathcal{M}}$. The solver takes the thermochemistry from NASA CEA at
the motor's chamber pressure and writes the value it used under each box: at
40~bar $T_c$ 1696.0~K, $\mathcal{M}$ 42.145~g/mol, $\gamma$ 1.1206, $c^*$
914.5~m/s. The values in the catalogue row (915.9~m/s, 1713.1~K) are the
record's single-pressure values and are not sent. With 95\,\% combustion
efficiency the delivered $c^*$ is 869~m/s.

In a solid motor the burning area sets the chamber pressure. With the ratio of
burning surface to throat area $K_n = A_b/A_t$, the equilibrium pressure is
$P_c = (K_n\,a\,\rho_p\,c^*)^{1/(1-n)}$. In the example \ui{Kn (initial)} is
222 and \ui{Kn (final)} is 210; in a BATES grain the bore surface grows while
the end faces shrink, and the curve becomes progressive-regressive. The line
under the thrust-curve chart names the shape. The throat is given with two
diameters: machined 18.40~mm and effective (with discharge coefficient)
18.22~mm.

\ekran{img/v3_0_5/kati_sonuc_ozet_en.png}{\ui{PERFORMANCE SUMMARY} of the solid example and the two-phase status band: the Isp carries no verified two-phase correction.}{fig:u2-ozet}

\ekran{img/v3_0_5/kati_itki_egrisi_en.png}{Thrust curve of the solid example: progressive-regressive shape and the regime-boundary note.}{fig:u2-itki}

\subsection{Declarations: two-phase flow, throat erosion, burn-rate regime}

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering\small
\caption{\ui{CHECK} lines of the solid example and how to read them}\label{tab:u2-kontrol}
\begin{tabular}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{6.2cm}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{9.4cm}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Line (summary)} & \textbf{Meaning} \\
\midrule
The published Isp carries no verified two-phase correction. & KNDX products contain a condensed phase (K\textsubscript{2}CO\textsubscript{3}); the particle-lag loss is not verified for this state and the applied two-phase efficiency is 1. Do not read this Isp as verified delivered performance. \\
Throat erosion is not modelled in this run: the area would grow by about 9.1\,\% (threshold 5\,\%). & The graphite throat wears during the burn; wear lowers chamber pressure and thrust. The number is an estimate. \\
The throat erosion law is extrapolated at this pressure (the law was measured for 69--450~bar). & The estimate above carries a large uncertainty. \\
Secondary coefficients (erosive burning, grain mechanics) are inherited from the sugar family record. & A family estimate, not KNDX-specific data. \\
Piecewise burn-rate law active with 5 pressure regimes. & A regime table replaces a single $a$--$n$ pair. A chart note marks the moment the curve touches a regime boundary (25.7~bar in this example). \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\ekran{img/v3_0_5/kati_uyarilar_en.png}{\ui{WARNINGS} of the solid example: five \ui{CHECK} lines (Table~\ref{tab:u2-kontrol}).}{fig:u2-uyari}

\subsection{Changing one input: design pressure 40 → 50~bar}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.6em]
  \item In the \ui{4. NOZZLE} section type 50 in \ui{Chamber Pressure (bar)}.
  \item Press \ui{Calculate Motor Performance}.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering\small
\caption{Effect of the design pressure (solid example, from the screen)}\label{tab:u2-pc}
\begin{tabular}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{5.0cm}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{3.2cm}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{3.2cm}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Quantity} & \textbf{40~bar} & \textbf{50~bar} \\
\midrule
Sea-level / vacuum Isp & 125.3 / 141.5~s & 128.5 / 144.3~s \\
Average / peak thrust & 1299 / 1498~N & 1554 / 1795~N \\
Burn time & 2.28~s & 1.95~s \\
Thrust coefficient & 1.41 & 1.45 \\
Propellant mass & 2.41~kg & 2.41~kg \\
Total impulse (card) & 3.0~kN·s & 3.0~kN·s \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

A higher design pressure gives a smaller throat and a higher $K_n$. Because the
burn rate $r = a\,P^n$ rises with pressure, the web burns out sooner: the burn
time shortens and thrust rises. The grain is unchanged, so the propellant mass
is unchanged; total impulse is propellant mass times Isp, and the 2.5\,\% rise
in Isp is not visible at the resolution of the card. The Isp gain comes from
the higher pressure ratio ($P_c/P_a$). The cost of the higher pressure is the
load on the case and closure; the wall and closure rows are resized
accordingly.

\ekran{img/v3_0_5/kati_pc50_ozet_en.png}{\ui{PERFORMANCE SUMMARY} of the solid example at a design pressure of 50~bar: burn time 1.95~s, average thrust 1554~N. Note that the propellant mass (2.41~kg) is unchanged.}{fig:u2-pc50}

\subsection{Analysis Dock: the Structural Safety panel}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.6em]
  \item In the \ui{ANALYSIS DOCK} open the \ui{STRUCTURAL} tab.
  \item The \ui{Wall Thickness (m)} field of the \ui{Structural Safety} panel
  is filled with the wall sized by the main calculation (0.002~m in the
  example, \ui{COMPUTED} badge). Press \ui{Run Analysis}.
  \item Read the verdict line: the panel states \ui{STRUCTURE: NOT\_EVALUATED},
  \ui{VERDICT WITHHELD} and \ui{WALL: SIZED BY HRMA}. The reason under
  \ui{Why no acceptance was issued} is \ui{The safety factor could not be
  earned: the analysis compared the wall against a thickness it had sized
  itself}: HRMA does not approve a wall it has sized itself.
  \item For a verification run, enter the thickness of the wall to be
  manufactured in the \ui{Wall Thickness (m)} field and run the panel again.
  The badge becomes \ui{WALL: AS SUPPLIED} and the entered wall is checked
  against the design pressure. If the wall misses the safety target a verdict
  is issued (\ui{VERDICT ISSUED}, \ui{STRUCTURE: UNSAFE}). If it meets the
  target, the response as a whole is still not accepted, because the closure
  and nozzle stations are not verified in this panel: the verdict stays
  \ui{VERDICT WITHHELD} and the stations not verified are listed under
  \ui{Why no acceptance was issued}.
\end{enumerate}

\ekran{img/v3_0_5/kati_guverte_yapisal_en.png}{\ui{Structural Safety} panel of the solid example after the run: inputs, value-source badges and the verdict line (\ui{VERDICT WITHHELD}, \ui{WALL: SIZED BY HRMA}).}{fig:u2-yapisal}

The panel inputs are in Table~\ref{tab:p-yapisal}. The bore-strain check
specific to solid motors is in the \ui{Grain Section FEA} panel
(Section~\ref{sec:guverte}).

\subsection{Grain support and bore strain}

The example's \ui{Grain Support} field is \ui{Cartridge-loaded (free-standing)}:
the grain is cast outside the case and inserted, and cure shrinkage is not
restrained (NASA SP-8073). The \ui{Structural Analysis} tab of the \ui{Motor
Specifications} card then gives a bore strain of 0.376\,\%, a strain safety
factor of 5.319 and a crack propagation risk of \ui{Low}. If the same grain is
set to \ui{Case-bonded}, the case restrains cure and cool-down shrinkage and the
bore carries that thermal strain on top of the pressure strain. Measured
result: bore strain 2.209\,\%, strain safety factor 0.906, crack propagation
risk \ui{High}; a \ui{CHECK} line for bore cracking risk is added to the
\ui{WARNINGS}. The strain capability (2\,\%) is a literature-band input, not
measured on the batch; measure the propellant before accepting the grain. The
field changes only the grain structural results; the ballistic numbers stay the
same.

\subsection{Purpose}

Read the cycle card, the wall temperatures of regenerative cooling, the RP-1
carbon-deposit declarations and the NASA CEA comparison on the liquid example;
see the effect of O/F on the wall limit. The full input list is in
Tables~\ref{tab:sivi-1}--\ref{tab:sivi-yorunge}.

\subsection{The example}

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering\small
\caption{Main inputs of the liquid example (\kod{Example Liquid LOX-RP1 25kN})}\label{tab:u3-girdi}
\begin{tabular}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{5.4cm}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{3.8cm}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{6.4cm}@{}}
\toprule

\subsection{Performance and cycle}

\ui{Performance Summary}: \ui{SEA LEVEL ISP} 257.1~s, \ui{VACUUM ISP} 301.1~s,
\ui{SPACE OPTIMIZED ISP} 316.7~s (same chamber, vacuum expansion ratio 30),
\ui{VACUUM THRUST} 29.3~kN. Mass flow 9.915~kg/s (oxidizer 6.610, fuel
3.305~kg/s), throat diameter 66.92~mm, exit diameter 231.82~mm, delivered
$c^*$ 1738.3~m/s, chamber temperature 3328~K. The \ui{Engine Specifications} card gives the
optimum O/F as 2.568; the example deliberately runs at 2.0
(Section~\ref{sec:u3-of}).

The difference between sea-level and vacuum Isp comes from the exit pressure:
at $\varepsilon = 12$ the exit pressure is 0.474~bar, below ambient; the
nozzle is overexpanded at sea level and loses $(P_e - P_a)A_e$ of thrust.

The \ui{Engine Cycle, Throttle \& Pressurization} card gives the power balance
of the gas-generator cycle (\ui{Converged}), the pump discharge pressures
(oxidizer 73, fuel 76~bar) and the open-cycle Isp loss (2.3~s). The
\ui{Throttle map} lists five points from 40\,\% to 100\,\%; the 40\,\% point
reads \ui{marginal margin}. The throttle note also states that below 85.5\,\%
of thrust the nozzle would separate at sea level and that the sea-level Isp of
those points is not published.

\ekran{img/v3_0_5/sivi_cevrim_kisma_en.png}{\ui{Engine Cycle, Throttle \& Pressurization}: power balance, pump discharge pressures and the chug-margin column of the throttle map.}{fig:u3-cevrim}

\subsection{Cooling and carbon deposits}

RP-1 leaves a carbon deposit on the hot wall. The deposit is a thermal
resistance: it insulates the wall and lowers the hot-face temperature. If it
spalls, the wall underneath sees the deposit-free heat flux. HRMA computes both
cases:

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering\small
\caption{Wall temperatures of the liquid example (from the warning lines)}\label{tab:u3-cidar}
\begin{tabular}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{6.0cm}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{2.4cm}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{7.2cm}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Quantity} & \textbf{Value} & \textbf{Comparison} \\
\midrule
Peak hot wall, with deposit & 613~K & Below the CuCrZr allowable. \\
Hot wall where the deposit spalls & 1341~K & CuCrZr melts at 1349~K; the margin is narrow. \\
Coolant-side wall (RP-1 face) & 603~K & Above the 561~K coking warning level, below the 728~K NASA SP-8087 design criterion. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Staying below 728~K does not show that the wall stays deposit-free; the screen
says so at the end of the line. The deposit resistance is modelled for LOX/RP-1
inside the NASA TP-2862 envelope (O/F 1.77--3.32, $P_c$ 4.1--13.8~MPa); outside
it the result is declared out of envelope.

\ekran{img/v3_0_5/sivi_uyarilar_en.png}{\ui{WARNINGS} of the liquid example: carbon deposit, coking risk and \ui{INPUT} lines.}{fig:u3-uyari}

\subsection{Changing one input: O/F 2.0 → 2.1}\label{sec:u3-of}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.6em]
  \item In the \ui{2. O/F OPTIMIZATION DATA} section type 2.1 in \ui{Target
  Mixture Ratio (O/F)}.
  \item Press \ui{Calculate Engine Performance}.
\end{enumerate}

Sea-level Isp rises from 257.1 to 260.0~s and vacuum Isp from 301.1 to
304.2~s: O/F has moved towards the optimum (2.568). A \ui{CRITICAL} line is
added to the warning list, stating that where the carbon deposit spalls the hot
wall reaches 1382~K, above the 1349~K melting point of CuCrZr (C18150, aged),
which means local liner damage. Higher O/F means hotter gas and higher heat
flux; for a 1.0~mm CuCrZr liner the valid point is O/F 2.0. Moving the design
to O/F 2.1 requires revisiting the cooling (channel geometry, coolant flow) or
the liner. Set the value back to 2.0.

\section{Workflow: from Requirement to Detailed Analysis}\label{sec:akis}

\subsection{Flow}

A new motor is developed in the following order. The section used in each step
is given in parentheses. The basis of the first decisions (mixture ratio,
chamber pressure, expansion ratio, characteristic length, injector pressure
drop) is given in Section~\ref{sec:yontem}.

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.6em]
  \item \textbf{Requirement.} Derive thrust, burn time or total impulse, the
  envelope (diameter, length) and the mass limit from the mission. In total
  impulse mode give either thrust or burn time; the other is solved from
  $I_t = F\,t_b$ (Table~\ref{tab:hib-temel}).
  \item \textbf{Motor type and propellant pair.} Choose the page; enter the
  propellant pair and mixture ratio. A propellant not in the catalogue is
  rejected by name.
  \item \textbf{Operating point.} Enter chamber pressure and expansion ratio (or
  design altitude); ratios left empty are solved by the model and reported in
  the warnings.
  \item \textbf{Calculation.} \ui{Calculate}. Read the strip at the top of the
  results (items not modelled), then the headline numbers, then the warnings
  (Section~\ref{sec:hukumler}).
  \item \textbf{Analysis.} The Analysis Dock and Analysis Center panels are
  filled from the last calculation; run the relevant panels
  (Section~\ref{sec:guverte}).
  \item \textbf{Revision.} Resolve a \ui{CRITICAL} line with the change it
  proposes; follow the effect in the dock's \ui{What changed} block or in the
  \ui{Comparative Analysis} panel. Each revision can be kept as a separate
  project with \ui{Save As}.
  \item \textbf{Verification inputs.} Enter known values such as the wall
  thickness to be manufactured, a measured $c^*$ efficiency, regression or
  burn-rate coefficients; HRMA then runs a verification instead of a proposal.
  \item \textbf{CAD.} Obtain STEP, STL, DXF and drawings
  (Section~\ref{sec:disaaktarim}). Drawing dimensions are the geometry of the
  main calculation.
  \item \textbf{Transfer to detailed analysis.} Take the STEP model to CAD and
  finite-element software and the \kod{.eng} file to flight simulation. The PDF
  report carries the source of every number and the items not modelled.
  \item \textbf{Test.} Before flight, carry out physical testing (static
  firing); compare the measured thrust curve with the HRMA prediction in the
  \ui{User Data Validation} panel.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Choosing the design parameters}\label{sec:yontem}

The first decisions of a preliminary design are the mixture ratio, the chamber
pressure, the expansion ratio, the characteristic length and the injector
pressure drop. For each of them the subsections below give three things: the
relation that governs the choice and its source, what HRMA does when the field
is left empty, and the effect measured on the shipped examples. A range is
written only when it rests on a published source; the sources are listed in
Table~\ref{tab:yontem-kaynak}.

\subsubsection{Mixture ratio (O/F)}

The mixture ratio that maximises Isp lies below the stoichiometric ratio, on the
fuel-rich side: the flame temperature drops slightly, the mean molar mass of the
products drops more, and $c^* \propto \sqrt{T_c/\mathcal{M}}$ rises (Sutton and
Biblarz, Ch.~5). HRMA scans this ratio from thermochemistry. On the liquid page
the \ui{Engine Specifications} card states the optimum O/F (2.568 in the liquid
example); on the hybrid page the \ui{Find Optimum} button finds the ratio that
maximises Isp for the selected propellant pair.

The optimum O/F need not be the design point. As the ratio approaches
stoichiometric, flame temperature and wall heat flux rise; the material limit
of the wall or of the nozzle throat also governs the choice, and HRMA states
that limit with its number in the warning list. Effect measured on the
examples:

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em]
  \item Liquid example, O/F 2.0 → 2.1: sea-level Isp 257.1 → 260.0~s; hot wall
  where the carbon deposit spalls 1341 → 1382~K, CuCrZr melting point 1349~K;
  \ui{CRITICAL} (Section~\ref{sec:u3-of}).
  \item Hybrid example, O/F 6.0 → 7.0: Isp 209.8 → 210.1~s; throat wall
  3304~K, allowable temperature of graphite 3300~K; \ui{CRITICAL}
  (Section~\ref{sec:u1-of}).
\end{itemize}

In both examples the Isp gain is small (1.1\,\% in the liquid example,
0.1\,\% in the hybrid) and a material limit is exceeded; this is why the
examples run below the optimum. In a solid motor O/F
is not a design variable: the ratio is the composition of the propellant and
comes from the catalogue record.

\subsubsection{Chamber pressure}

Chamber pressure changes several quantities together. The relations HRMA uses:

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em]
  \item Throat area $A_t = \dot m\,c^*/P_c$: at the same flow a higher pressure
  gives a smaller throat and a smaller motor.
  \item At the same ambient pressure a larger $P_c/P_a$ allows a larger matched
  expansion ratio and a larger $C_F$ (Sutton and Biblarz, Ch.~3).
  \item The gas-side heat transfer coefficient rises with $(P_c/c^*)^{0.8}$
  (Bartz 1957); the cooling and liner load grow with pressure.
  \item In a thin wall the hoop stress $\sigma_\theta = P_c\,D/(2t)$ rises
  linearly with pressure; for the same safety factor the wall thickness and
  mass grow.
\end{itemize}

In a solid motor the chamber pressure is set by the burning area ($K_n$,
Section~\ref{sec:uyg-kati}); the burn rate depends on pressure through
$r = a\,P^n$. In the solid example raising the design pressure from 40 to
50~bar shortens the burn time from 2.28 to 1.95~s and raises the average thrust
from 1299 to 1554~N and the sea-level Isp from 125.3 to 128.5~s
(Table~\ref{tab:u2-pc}). In a hybrid fed by self-pressurised
N\textsubscript{2}O the vapour pressure of the tank caps the chamber pressure:
the injector drop is the tank pressure minus the chamber pressure
(Table~\ref{tab:u1-uyari}).

\subsubsection{Expansion ratio}

At a given ambient pressure thrust is largest when the nozzle exit pressure
equals the ambient pressure ($P_e = P_a$) (Sutton and Biblarz, Ch.~3). If
\ui{Ae/At Ratio} is left at 0 on the hybrid page, HRMA solves this ratio from
the isentropic relation for the ambient pressure of the design altitude
(example: 5.0364) and states it in the warning list. At zero ambient pressure
(vacuum) the matched ratio is unbounded; HRMA computes no ratio in this case and asks
for the field by name. A vacuum nozzle is sized by mass and envelope.

A large-ratio nozzle operating at sea level is over-expanded and loses
$(P_e - P_a)A_e$ of thrust (liquid example: $\varepsilon = 12$, $P_e$ =
0.474~bar). When the wall pressure falls below about 0.4 times the ambient
pressure the flow separates from the wall (Summerfield criterion; HRMA factor
0.40, literature band 0.35--0.40). For this reason the throttle note of the
liquid example publishes no sea-level Isp for points below 85.5\,\% thrust
(Section~\ref{sec:uyg-sivi}).

\subsubsection{Characteristic length (L*)}

$L^* = V_c/A_t$ sets the residence time of the combustion gas in the chamber. A
short L* leaves combustion incomplete; a long L* adds mass and thermal load.
The liquid page takes L* per propellant pair from the table of Huzel and Huang
(NASA SP-125, Ch.~IV, Table~4-1, p.~87; inch values converted to metres).

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering\small
\caption{L* bands of the liquid page per propellant pair (NASA SP-125, Table 4-1)}\label{tab:lstar}
\begin{tabular}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{7.0cm}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{3.0cm}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{3.0cm}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Propellant pair} & \textbf{L* (m)} & \textbf{SP-125 (in)} \\
\midrule
LOX / RP-1 & 1.02--1.27 & 40--50 \\
LOX / LH\textsubscript{2} (liquid hydrogen injection) & 0.76--1.02 & 30--40 \\
LOX / NH\textsubscript{3} & 0.76--1.02 & 30--40 \\
N\textsubscript{2}O\textsubscript{4} / MMH, UDMH, hydrazine, A-50 & 0.76--0.89 & 30--35 \\
RFNA, IRFNA / hydrazine, MMH, UDMH & 0.76--0.89 & 30--35 \\
H\textsubscript{2}O\textsubscript{2} / RP-1 (with catalyst bed) & 1.52--1.78 & 60--70 \\
LF\textsubscript{2} / LH\textsubscript{2} & 0.56--0.76 & 22--30 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

If the field is empty HRMA uses the midpoint of the band and states the band
with its source. For a pair not in the table the general range of the SP-125
text (0.38--3.05~m; residence time 0.002--0.040~s) is declared; it is not a
pair-specific value. The liquid example uses an L* of 1.2~m, inside the
LOX/RP-1 band.

In a hybrid motor most of the chamber volume is the port of the fuel grain. In
the example the requested L* is 1.0~m and the reached one 7.72~m
(Table~\ref{tab:u1-cikti}): the grain length follows from the regression rate
and the O/F, and L* is not the quantity that sizes this design.

\subsubsection{Injector pressure drop ($\Delta P/P_c$)}

The injector pressure drop decouples the feed system from pressure oscillations
in the chamber. The classical design band is 15--25\,\% of chamber pressure
(Sutton and Biblarz, Ch.~8; NASA SP-194, Ch.~5--6): below 0.15 the feed system
can couple with the chamber in a low-frequency instability (chug), 0.20 is the
recommended value, and a drop above 0.25 is paid for in feed pressure and pump
work. The band is a design rule, not a sharp physical boundary.

If \ui{Injector Pressure Drop} is left empty on the liquid page, the drop is
the chamber pressure times the ratio of the element type (unlike impinging
0.22, coaxial 0.18, showerhead 0.28, pintle 0.15, other types 0.20), and the
result states this with its source label. In the liquid example the drop is
20~bar at a chamber pressure of 50~bar: $\Delta P/P_c = 0.40$, above the band;
the injector schematic shows it as \ui{dP/Pc 40\%}. In a self-pressurised
hybrid the drop is not chosen; it follows from the tank and chamber pressures
(0.68 in the hybrid example).

\centering\small
\caption{Sources cited in this section}\label{tab:yontem-kaynak}
\begin{tabular}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{3.4cm}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{12.2cm}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Short form} & \textbf{Work} \\
\midrule
Sutton and Biblarz & G. P. Sutton, O. Biblarz, \emph{Rocket Propulsion Elements}, 9th ed., Wiley. Ch.~3 nozzles, Ch.~5 mixture ratio, Ch.~8 injectors. \\
NASA SP-125 & D. K. Huzel, D. H. Huang, \emph{Design of Liquid Propellant Rocket Engines}, NASA SP-125, 2nd ed., 1971. Ch.~IV, Table~4-1. \\
NASA SP-194 & D. T. Harrje, F. H. Reardon (eds.), \emph{Liquid Propellant Rocket Combustion Instability}, NASA SP-194, 1972. Ch.~5--6. \\

derives the case bore, and the migration is reported by a named load warning;
the file on disk is not changed.

\subsection{Common layout of a designer page}\label{sec:ortakyapi}

The three designer pages follow the same order.

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.6em]
  \item \textbf{Form.} Numbered or named sections; a ``?'' note next to every
  field (opened with the mouse, with Tab and Enter or Space from the keyboard,
  or by touch; Esc closes it).
  \item \textbf{Calculation button.} \ui{Calculate} on the hybrid page,
  \ui{Calculate Motor Performance} on the solid page, \ui{Calculate Engine
  Performance} on the liquid page. The hybrid and liquid pages also have
  analysis-type tabs: \ui{Single Point Analysis}, \ui{Parametric Analysis},
  \ui{Trajectory Analysis}; on the liquid page the tabs appear after the first
  calculation.
  \item \textbf{Design with AI.} The panel below the calculation button
  (Section~\ref{sec:yz}).
  \item \textbf{Results.} Performance summary, warnings, design tables,
  cross-section and charts, side panels, NASA CEA comparison.
  \item \textbf{Analysis Dock and Analysis Center} (Section~\ref{sec:guverte}).
  \item \textbf{Exports} (Section~\ref{sec:disaaktarim}).
\end{enumerate}

\ekran{img/v3_0_5/ipucu_acik_hibrit_cstar_en.png}{A field's ``?'' note open
(\ui{Combustion (c*) Efficiency}): what it is, its unit, its effect on the
calculation, what happens if blank, and the accepted range.}{fig:ipucu}

Each chart carries a ``what this shows'' note and a reading note. Charts are
interactive: hovering a point shows its value with units.

\subsection{Design with AI}\label{sec:yz}

HRMA calls no AI service. The panel is for a manual text exchange with an
assistant chosen by the user and also works before a calculation.

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.6em]
  \item Type the design goal in the panel's text area.
  \item Press \ui{Copy context}. The text carries the entire form (label,
  value, unit, accepted range, source, the solver's ``not used''
  declarations), the headline numbers if any, the warnings, the withheld
  verdicts and the CEA block. \ui{Show text} opens the same text in the panel.
  \item Paste the text into the assistant; paste the field values it proposes
  back into the panel.
  \item Press \ui{Check suggestion}. HRMA accepts only the page's own fields,
  as finite numbers or valid options; it rejects unit mismatches and
  out-of-range values by name and shows a before/after table with \ui{Apply}
  and \ui{Apply and calculate}.
  \item \ui{Copy continuation package} tells the assistant what changed and
  the new result.
\end{enumerate}

\ekran{img/v3_0_5/yapay_zeka_paneli_hibrit_en.png}{The \ui{Design with AI}
panel: design goal, \ui{Copy context} and \ui{Check suggestion}.}{fig:yz}

The assistant's suggestion is not a result; the calculation, the warnings and
the rejections decide.

% =====================================================================
\section{Hybrid Motor Page}\label{sec:hibrit}

\subsection{Purpose}

Sizes the design point, fuel grain, injector, nozzle and wall of a motor with
a liquid (or gaseous) oxidizer and a solid fuel (hybrid); solves thrust and
chamber pressure against time, port growth and O/F shift.

\subsection{Screen}

\ekran{img/v3_0_5/hibrit_form_temel_en.png}{Hybrid page: the \ui{BASIC
PARAMETERS} section. Note the \ui{Thrust \& Time} and \ui{Total Impulse}
design-mode tabs and the \ui{Tank Pressure Source} selector.}{fig:hib-form}

\subsection{Inputs}

Tables~\ref{tab:hib-bilgi}--\ref{tab:hib-yapilandirma} give every field of
the hybrid form in screen order. The \ui{Form limit} column is the browser
check; the server's canonical bands are in Appendix~\ref{sec:eke}. \ui{Form
default} is the value of an empty page; the example projects carry their own
values.

expansion ratio, combustion type, $c^*$ efficiency and residual web.}{fig:hib-ileri}

and the tank pressure source.}{fig:hib-oks}

\textbf{Thrust, $F$} & \texttt{thrust} & N & \ensuremath{\ge}\,1 & 1000 \\*
\multicolumn{5}{@{}p{\dimexpr\linewidth\relax}@{}}{\footnotesize \emph{Effect on the calculation:} Design-point thrust of the motor, in N. With the burn time it fixes the total impulse (I = F\ensuremath{\cdot}t\_b) and, through Isp, the mass flow and propellant masses. Accepted range 10-100000 N (form 1-100000, server 10-1000000). \emph{If blank:} Required: if it is left empty the run is rejected by name; no thrust is assumed.} \\ \midrule
\textbf{Burn Time, $t_b$} & \texttt{burn\_\allowbreak{}time} & s & \ensuremath{\ge}\,0.1 & 10 \\*
\multicolumn{5}{@{}p{\dimexpr\linewidth\relax}@{}}{\footnotesize \emph{Effect on the calculation:} Design burn time, in s. With the thrust it fixes the total impulse (I = F\ensuremath{\cdot}t\_b) and so the propellant masses and the fuel grain. Accepted range 0.1-300 s. \emph{If blank:} Required: if it is left empty the run is rejected by name; no burn time is assumed.} \\ \midrule
\textbf{Total Impulse (Newton\ensuremath{\cdot}seconds), $I_t$} & \texttt{total\_\allowbreak{}impulse} & N\ensuremath{\cdot}s & 1000 -- 1000000 & 10000 \\*
\multicolumn{5}{@{}p{\dimexpr\linewidth\relax}@{}}{\footnotesize \emph{Effect on the calculation:} Total impulse the motor must deliver, in N\ensuremath{\cdot}s (I = F\ensuremath{\cdot}t\_b at the design point). It fixes the propellant masses through Isp. With thrust given, the burn time is solved; with burn time given, the thrust is solved. Required in this mode. Form range 1000-1000000 N\ensuremath{\cdot}s; a solved thrust or burn time outside its own band is rejected by name.} \\ \midrule
\textbf{Thrust, $F$} & \texttt{thrust\_\allowbreak{}impulse} & N & 100 -- 100000 & (blank) \\*
\multicolumn{5}{@{}p{\dimexpr\linewidth\relax}@{}}{\footnotesize \emph{Effect on the calculation:} Design-point thrust, in N. In total-impulse mode give this OR the burn time: the other is solved from I = F\ensuremath{\cdot}t\_b. Form range 100-100000 N. \emph{If blank:} If both are empty the run is rejected by name; HRMA does not pick an 'optimal' thrust.} \\ \midrule
\textbf{Burn Time, $t_b$} & \texttt{burn\_\allowbreak{}time\_\allowbreak{}impulse} & s & 1 -- 300 & (blank) \\*
\multicolumn{5}{@{}p{\dimexpr\linewidth\relax}@{}}{\footnotesize \emph{Effect on the calculation:} Design burn time, in s. In total-impulse mode give this OR the thrust: the other is solved from I = F\ensuremath{\cdot}t\_b. Form range 1-300 s. \emph{If blank:} If both are empty the run is rejected by name.} \\ \midrule
\textbf{Chamber Pressure (absolute), $P_c$} & \texttt{chamber\_\allowbreak{}pressure} & bar & \ensuremath{\ge}\,1 & 20 \\*
\multicolumn{5}{@{}p{\dimexpr\linewidth\relax}@{}}{\footnotesize \emph{Effect on the calculation:} The combustion chamber pressure in bar. Higher pressures generally increase specific impulse but require stronger structures.} \\ \midrule
\textbf{Tank Pressure Source} & \texttt{tank\_\allowbreak{}pressure\_\allowbreak{}source} &  &  & Self-pressurised: P\_sat(T\_tank) \\*
\multicolumn{5}{@{}p{\dimexpr\linewidth\relax}@{}}{\footnotesize \emph{Effect on the calculation:} Where the injector feed pressure comes from. Oxidizer default: self-pressurising N\textsubscript{2}O uses P\_sat(T\_tank); LOX/H\textsubscript{2}O\textsubscript{2} use the design pressure-drop ratio. User-supplied tank pressure: for a supercharged (He/N\textsubscript{2}) N\textsubscript{2}O tank or a pressure-fed LOX/H\textsubscript{2}O\textsubscript{2} tank; the tank pressure you enter becomes the injector inlet pressure. In this mode the self-pressurised tank blowdown history is not published (pressurant expansion and dissolution are not modelled); only the design point is computed. Options: Self-pressurised: P\_sat(T\_tank); User-supplied tank pressure.} \\ \midrule
\textbf{Tank Pressure (absolute), $P_{tank}$} & \texttt{tank\_\allowbreak{}pressure} & bar & \ensuremath{\ge}\,1 & (blank) \\*
\multicolumn{5}{@{}p{\dimexpr\linewidth\relax}@{}}{\footnotesize \emph{Effect on the calculation:} Oxidizer tank pressure (absolute). How it is used depends on the Tank Pressure Source: with the oxidizer default the field is read-only and shows, after a calculation, the feed pressure the injector circuit used (self-pressurising N\textsubscript{2}O: the saturation pressure at the oxidizer temperature, P\_sat(T\_tank); LOX/H\textsubscript{2}O\textsubscript{2}: P\_c\ensuremath{\cdot}(1 + \ensuremath{\Delta}P/P\_c) from the design pressure-drop ratio). With User-supplied tank pressure the value you enter feeds the injector circuit (P\_1 = P\_tank, feed line loss not included) and must exceed the chamber pressure; for N\textsubscript{2}O it must also be at least P\_sat(T\_tank).} \\ \midrule
\end{longtable}}

\textbf{L* Value (characteristic length), $L^*$} & \texttt{l\_\allowbreak{}star} & m & \ensuremath{\ge}\,0.1 & (blank) \\*
\multicolumn{5}{@{}p{\dimexpr\linewidth\relax}@{}}{\footnotesize \emph{Effect on the calculation:} Characteristic length - ratio of combustion chamber volume to throat area. Determines residence time for complete combustion. Higher values ensure complete combustion but increase motor weight.} \\ \midrule
\textbf{Initial Port Diameter, $D_{p,0}$} & \texttt{initial\_\allowbreak{}port\_\allowbreak{}diameter} & mm & 0 -- 500 & 0 \\*
\multicolumn{5}{@{}p{\dimexpr\linewidth\relax}@{}}{\footnotesize \emph{Effect on the calculation:} Starting fuel grain port diameter. Drives initial oxidizer mass flux, regression rate and the whole thrust-time curve. Leave 0 to size the port automatically from the design mass flux (350 kg/m2.s, or the chamber Gox you enter under finite combustion). \emph{If blank:} 0 = auto} \\ \midrule
\textbf{Number of Ports empty = 1 port, $N_p$} & \texttt{port\_\allowbreak{}count} &  & \ensuremath{\ge}\,1 & (blank) \\*
\multicolumn{5}{@{}p{\dimexpr\linewidth\relax}@{}}{\footnotesize \emph{Effect on the calculation:} Number of equivalent circular combustion ports in the fuel grain. It scales the burning area, the port flow area and the acoustic mode count, so it changes thrust, chamber pressure and the stability verdict. Above one port the solver states that port interaction, web thickness and burn-through are not modelled. \emph{If blank:} Leave empty for a single port.} \\ \midrule
\textbf{Ae/At Ratio expansion ratio, 0=auto, $\varepsilon$} & \texttt{expansion\_\allowbreak{}ratio} &  & \ensuremath{\ge}\,0 & (blank) \\*
\multicolumn{5}{@{}p{\dimexpr\linewidth\relax}@{}}{\footnotesize \emph{Effect on the calculation:} Nozzle exit area to throat area ratio. Higher ratios provide better performance at altitude but increase nozzle size. Set to 0 for automatic optimization.} \\ \midrule
\textbf{Nozzle Type} & \texttt{nozzle\_\allowbreak{}type} &  &  & Conical Nozzle \\*
\multicolumn{5}{@{}p{\dimexpr\linewidth\relax}@{}}{\footnotesize \emph{Effect on the calculation:} Nozzle geometry type. Bell: optimized contour, maximum performance, more complex manufacturing. Bell nozzles provide higher efficiency. Options: Conical Nozzle; Bell Nozzle; Parabolic Nozzle.} \\ \midrule
\textbf{Combustion Type} & \texttt{combustion\_\allowbreak{}type} &  &  & Infinite Area Combustion \\*
\multicolumn{5}{@{}p{\dimexpr\linewidth\relax}@{}}{\footnotesize \emph{Effect on the calculation:} Chamber model of the equilibrium solution. Infinite area: the chamber cross-section is treated as infinite, so the gas enters the nozzle at rest and the injector-face pressure is the nozzle stagnation pressure. Finite area: with a finite contraction ratio the gas is accelerated in the chamber by combustion and loses stagnation pressure (Rayleigh flow), so the nozzle inlet stagnation pressure is lower; it needs a contraction ratio or chamber mass flux. Neither option models mixing. Options: Infinite Area Combustion; Finite Area Combustion.} \\ \midrule
\textbf{Combustion (c*) Efficiency, $\eta_{c^*}$} & \texttt{combustion\_\allowbreak{}efficiency} & \% & 50 -- 105 & (blank) \\*
\multicolumn{5}{@{}p{\dimexpr\linewidth\relax}@{}}{\footnotesize \emph{Effect on the calculation:} Delivered c* as a percentage of the theoretical equilibrium c* (eta\_c*). It scales c* and with it Isp, mass flow, propellant masses, grain length and the transient / tank blowdown curves; the throat area is set by thrust, chamber pressure and C\_F and does not change. Accepted range 50-105 \%; a value outside it is rejected, not clipped. \emph{If blank:} Left empty: N2O/HTPB uses the median of 26 measured firings in HRMA's validation records, 89 \% (range 77-99 \%; Heydari 2017, Scaramuzzino/Carmicino 2013); other propellant pairs have no measured value in HRMA, so the ideal c* is used (no efficiency applied) and the result says so.} \\ \midrule
\textbf{Chamber Diameter, $D_c$} & \texttt{chamber\_\allowbreak{}diameter\_\allowbreak{}input} & mm & \ensuremath{\ge}\,0 & (blank) \\*
\multicolumn{5}{@{}p{\dimexpr\linewidth\relax}@{}}{\footnotesize \emph{Effect on the calculation:} Inner diameter of the combustion chamber, equal to the fuel grain outer diameter (liner/insulation is not modelled). Left at 0, HRMA sizes the grain to the end-of-burn ports: one port: final port diameter + 2 x residual web; N ports: single ring of final ports touching each other and the wall, final port x (1 + 1/sin(180\ensuremath{^\circ}/N)) + 2 x residual web. A diameter you enter is kept; if the final ports do not fit in it the request is rejected with the minimum diameter, and the unburned fuel left outside the ports is reported. \emph{If blank:} 0=auto} \\ \midrule
\textbf{Residual Web Thickness, $w_r$} & \texttt{residual\_\allowbreak{}web\_\allowbreak{}thickness} & mm & \ensuremath{\ge}\,0 & (blank) \\*
\multicolumn{5}{@{}p{\dimexpr\linewidth\relax}@{}}{\footnotesize \emph{Effect on the calculation:} Fuel web kept between the end-of-burn port(s) and the grain outer surface. It adds 2 x this value to the grain outer diameter. \emph{If blank:} Empty means 0: zero nominal residual fuel, an idealised sizing default; thermal protection (liner/insulation) and regression uncertainty are not included, and the port is modelled as axially uniform, so local burn-through near the aft end is not captured.} \\ \midrule
\textbf{Contraction Ratio Ac/At, $\varepsilon_c$} & \texttt{contraction\_\allowbreak{}ratio} &  & 0 -- 10 & (blank) \\*
\multicolumn{5}{@{}p{\dimexpr\linewidth\relax}@{}}{\footnotesize \emph{Effect on the calculation:} Ratio of combustion chamber cross-sectional area to throat area. Higher ratios reduce oxidizer velocity in chamber, affecting mixing and combustion efficiency. Set to 0 for automatic calculation.} \\ \midrule
\textbf{Mass Flux (Gox in chamber), $G$} & \texttt{mass\_\allowbreak{}flux\_\allowbreak{}chamber} & kg/\allowbreak{}m\textsuperscript{2}\ensuremath{\cdot}s & 0 -- 1000 & 0 \\*
\multicolumn{5}{@{}p{\dimexpr\linewidth\relax}@{}}{\footnotesize \emph{Effect on the calculation:} Oxidizer mass flow rate per unit area in the combustion chamber. Affects fuel regression rate and combustion efficiency. Higher flux increases regression but may cause incomplete combustion.} \\ \midrule
\end{longtable}}

HRMA's hybrid solver uses the TOTAL mass flux G\_total = (\ensuremath{\dot m}\_ox + \ensuremath{\dot m}\_f)/A\_port by default, not the oxidizer flux G\_ox. A literature a fitted against G\_ox therefore predicts about 10-18 \% higher regression here (HRMA propellant database note). \emph{If blank:} Empty: the selected fuel's tabulated value is used.} \\ \midrule
\textbf{Regression Rate Exponent (n), $n$} & \texttt{regression\_\allowbreak{}n} & - & 0.1 -- 1.0 & 0.555 \\*
\multicolumn{5}{@{}p{\dimexpr\linewidth\relax}@{}}{\footnotesize \emph{Effect on the calculation:} Power law exponent in regression rate equation r = a \ensuremath{\times} G\textasciicircum{}n. Determines sensitivity to oxidizer mass flux. Lower values (0.3-0.5) provide more stable combustion, higher values (0.6-0.8) are more mass flux sensitive.} \\ \midrule
\end{longtable}}

\textbf{Temperature, $T_{ox}$} & \texttt{oxidizer\_\allowbreak{}temp} & K & 182.33 -- 309.52 & 293 \\*
\multicolumn{5}{@{}p{\dimexpr\linewidth\relax}@{}}{\footnotesize \emph{Effect on the calculation:} Oxidizer temperature at storage/injection conditions. Affects density, viscosity, and vapor pressure. Room temperature: 293K (20\ensuremath{^\circ}C). Critical for accurate property calculations and system design.} \\ \midrule
\textbf{Oxidizer Feed Line Length} & \texttt{feed\_\allowbreak{}line\_\allowbreak{}length\_\allowbreak{}m} & m & 0.05 -- 50 & (blank) \\*
\multicolumn{5}{@{}p{\dimexpr\linewidth\relax}@{}}{\footnotesize \emph{Effect on the calculation:} Oxidizer feed-line length from the tank outlet to the injector manifold. Together with the inner diameter it sets the feed-line inertance, which switches the chug (low-frequency) stability loop to its second-order form. \emph{If blank:} Leave empty if unknown - the chug analysis then runs without line inertia and declares that assumption instead of guessing a layout.} \\ \midrule
\textbf{Oxidizer Feed Line Inner Diameter} & \texttt{feed\_\allowbreak{}line\_\allowbreak{}inner\_\allowbreak{}diameter\_\allowbreak{}mm} & mm & 0.5 -- 500 & (blank) \\*
\multicolumn{5}{@{}p{\dimexpr\linewidth\relax}@{}}{\footnotesize \emph{Effect on the calculation:} Inner diameter of the oxidizer feed line. The flow area for the feed-line inertance is derived from it as a circular duct. \emph{If blank:} Leave empty if unknown - the chug analysis then runs without line inertia and declares that assumption.} \\ \midrule
\end{longtable}}

\textbf{O/F Ratio oxidizer/fuel, O/F} & \texttt{of\_\allowbreak{}ratio} &  & \ensuremath{\ge}\,0.1 & 7.5 \\*
\multicolumn{5}{@{}p{\dimexpr\linewidth\relax}@{}}{\footnotesize \emph{Effect on the calculation:} Oxidizer-to-fuel mass ratio at the design point. Through the equilibrium solution it sets chamber temperature, c* and Isp; with the regression law it sizes the fuel grain. The maximum-Isp O/F depends on the propellant pair and chamber pressure: 'Find Optimum' solves it with the equilibrium solver for your chamber pressure. HRMA's in-repository reference table (a quoted design value, not a computed optimum) lists 7.5 for N2O/HTPB, 8.0 for N2O/paraffin and 2.3 for LOX/HTPB. Accepted range 0.5-20.} \\ \midrule

\toprule
\textbf{Input} & \textbf{Identifier} & \textbf{Unit} & \textbf{Form limit} & \textbf{Form default} \\ \midrule

\textbf{Injector Type} & \texttt{injector\_\allowbreak{}type} &  &  & Showerhead \\*
\multicolumn{5}{@{}p{\dimexpr\linewidth\relax}@{}}{\footnotesize \emph{Effect on the calculation:} How the oxidizer is injected. A hybrid has ONE liquid stream - the oxidizer; the fuel is the solid grain. Showerhead: parallel axial jets from a drilled plate. Impingement: like-on-like doublets - pairs of oxidizer jets that hit each other. Pintle: a central post with tip holes and an annular sheet. Swirl: pressure-swirl elements fed by tangential slots (hollow spray cone). Coaxial: one element with an inner jet and an outer annulus, both oxidizer. Showerhead, impingement, pintle and swirl are sized by the injector circuit solver; coaxial has no circuit model and is sized by the plate model alone. Options: Showerhead; Impingement; Pintle; Swirl; Coaxial.} \\ \midrule
\textbf{Injector Discharge Coefficient, $C_d$} & \texttt{discharge\_\allowbreak{}coefficient} & - & 0.20 -- 1.0 & (blank) \\*
\multicolumn{5}{@{}p{\dimexpr\linewidth\relax}@{}}{\footnotesize \emph{Effect on the calculation:} Discharge coefficient C\_d of the injector orifices. The orifice flow area is sized from it (mdot proportional to C\_d), so it changes hole count/diameter and the Nurick flip verdict. Ignored for swirl injectors, where C\_d is solved from geometry. \emph{If blank:} Leave empty to use the solver default of 0.78, which is then declared in the results instead of being silently assumed.} \\ \midrule
\textbf{Target Velocity, $v_{inj}$} & \texttt{target\_\allowbreak{}velocity} & m/s & \ensuremath{\ge}\,0 & (blank) \\*
\multicolumn{5}{@{}p{\dimexpr\linewidth\relax}@{}}{\footnotesize \emph{Effect on the calculation:} Mean oxidizer velocity through the holes that you would like to reach. It does not size the holes: the hole area follows from the oxidizer flow and the pressure drop solved by the injector circuit, so the results report the achieved velocity and the pressure drop your target would need. \emph{If blank:} Empty: 30 m/s is used for that comparison (server default, declared).} \\ \midrule
\textbf{Min Hole Diameter} & \texttt{hole\_\allowbreak{}diameter\_\allowbreak{}min} & mm & \ensuremath{\ge}\,0 & (blank) \\*
\multicolumn{5}{@{}p{\dimexpr\linewidth\relax}@{}}{\footnotesize \emph{Effect on the calculation:} Lower edge of the hole-diameter band the injector circuit plans in. The circuit uses the fewest holes whose diameter falls inside [min, max]; a hole count fixed in Injector Design overrides that search. \emph{If blank:} Empty: 0.5 mm (design band 0.5-2.5 mm, Sutton \& Biblarz 9th ed. p. 337; declared).} \\ \midrule
\textbf{Max Hole Diameter} & \texttt{hole\_\allowbreak{}diameter\_\allowbreak{}max} & mm & \ensuremath{\ge}\,0 & (blank) \\*
\multicolumn{5}{@{}p{\dimexpr\linewidth\relax}@{}}{\footnotesize \emph{Effect on the calculation:} Upper edge of the hole-diameter band the injector circuit plans in; it must be larger than the minimum. \emph{If blank:} Empty: 2.5 mm (design band 0.5-2.5 mm, Sutton \& Biblarz 9th ed. p. 337; declared).} \\ \midrule
\textbf{Plate Thickness, $t_{pl}$} & \texttt{plate\_\allowbreak{}thickness} & mm & \ensuremath{\ge}\,0 & (blank) \\*
\multicolumn{5}{@{}p{\dimexpr\linewidth\relax}@{}}{\footnotesize \emph{Effect on the calculation:} Thickness of the injector plate, i.e. the length of each orifice. It sets the orifice L/D, which picks the discharge coefficient C\_d and the hydraulic-flip verdict; the plate structural check also uses it. \emph{If blank:} Empty: the circuit keeps its declared L/D = 4 for C\_d and publishes no L/D or flip verdict.} \\ \midrule
\end{longtable}}

\textbf{Chamber Material} & \texttt{chamber\_\allowbreak{}material} &  &  & Stainless steel 304 (annealed) \\*
\multicolumn{5}{@{}p{\dimexpr\linewidth\relax}@{}}{\footnotesize \emph{Effect on the calculation:} Material of the combustion chamber case. The structural chain sizes or verifies the wall against hoop stress with the yield and ultimate strength of this material, derated at the computed wall temperature, and takes the chamber mass from its density. The heat-transfer chain uses its thermal conductivity for the wall temperature and its allowable temperature for the thermal verdict. The structural, safety and thermal panels of the analysis deck show the same material. Options: AISI 4130 low-alloy steel (normalized); Carbon steel (generic, A36-class); Stainless steel 304 (annealed); Stainless steel 316 (annealed); Aluminum 6061-T6; Titanium Ti-6Al-4V; Inconel 718 (aged); CuCrZr (C18150, aged); Aluminum 7075-T6; Aluminum 2024-T3; Stainless 17-4PH (H900); AISI 4340 low-alloy steel (normalized); Inconel 625 (annealed); Titanium CP Grade 2; Beryllium copper C17200 (aged, AT); Magnesium AZ31B-H24.} \\ \midrule
\textbf{Nozzle Material} & \texttt{nozzle\_\allowbreak{}material} &  &  & Graphite (isostatic, nozzle insert grade) \\*
\multicolumn{5}{@{}p{\dimexpr\linewidth\relax}@{}}{\footnotesize \emph{Effect on the calculation:} Material of the nozzle throat (insert). The throat thermal check solves the axial Bartz profile at the throat with the thermal conductivity and emissivity of this material, under the cooling assumption the motor assigns to it (shown below the selection), and compares the throat wall temperature with its allowable temperature. Throat erosion is computed only where a published erosion coefficient band exists (also shown below); otherwise a rigid throat is assumed and stated. The steady performance solution always assumes a rigid throat. Options: Graphite (isostatic, nozzle insert grade); Tungsten (wrought, stress-relieved); Carbon-carbon (2D/3D C-C); Molybdenum TZM (stress-relieved); Niobium C-103 (silicide coated); Copper (OFHC, annealed); CuCrZr (C18150, aged).} \\ \midrule
\textbf{Injector Material} & \texttt{injector\_\allowbreak{}material} &  &  & Not selected (plate check not run) \\*
\multicolumn{5}{@{}p{\dimexpr\linewidth\relax}@{}}{\footnotesize \emph{Effect on the calculation:} Material of the injector plate. Used only in the injector plate structural check: a clamped circular plate (Roark Table 11.2, case 10b) with ASME PG-52 ligament efficiency gives the bending stress, the safety factor and the required thickness from the room-temperature yield strength, and the plate mass from the density. With no material selected the plate check is not run. Options: Not selected (plate check not run); AISI 4130 low-alloy steel (normalized); Carbon steel (generic, A36-class); Stainless steel 304 (annealed); Stainless steel 316 (annealed); Aluminum 6061-T6; Titanium Ti-6Al-4V; Inconel 718 (aged); CuCrZr (C18150, aged); Aluminum 7075-T6; Aluminum 2024-T3; Stainless 17-4PH (H900); AISI 4340 low-alloy steel (normalized); Inconel 625 (annealed); Titanium CP Grade 2; Beryllium copper C17200 (aged, AT); Brass C36000 (free-cutting, H02); Magnesium AZ31B-H24.} \\ \midrule
\end{longtable}}
